evidence: Judged by visual event, not name: c1's event is a raked cast shadow of the contour thrown across a wall-and-floor continuum (shadow-as-second-silhouette); c3's event is a real object relationship at seated eye level between bottle, tabletop horizon and a vacant span of table (editorial hospitality narrative). These two are materially different planes of event. c2 and c4, however, stage the identical event: the untouched cutout centered in front of a neutral, diffusely lit backdrop that carries flat brand-colored graphics derived from the label (concentric script-echo lines vs. a single horizontal band), with the bottle static in front and typography limited to the same single pass. Swapping radiating line work for a horizontal band is a change of graphic motif and palette placement, not a change of concept; both read as 'isolated packshot plus decorative backdrop graphics.' Neither c2 nor c4 introduces a new plane, object relationship, narrative or perceptual mechanism beyond c1/c3's territory, and c4's occlusion gag is a property of the cutout's opacity that any backdrop graphic (including c2's rings passing behind the label) already exhibits. No impossible product modifications are proposed: all four preserve container, closure, label and liquid, invent no flavour/ingredient/nutrition claims, add no droplets to the cutout, and rely only on source-compatible generated surrounds consistent with the observed soft frontal illumination.
required_revision: Keep c1 and c3 as-is. Rebuild either c2 or c4 (recommend c4) so its visual event leaves the 'flat graphic on neutral backdrop behind a static packshot' family: move the event off the backdrop plane and into a perceptual or narrative mechanism, e.g. an editorial sequence where the script wordmark is completed by a real-world curve encountered in context (source-compatible photography), or a purposeful brand-graphic system in which the wordmark itself is reconstructed from negative space between two photographic elements, or an abstract metaphor where the contour is traced by a continuous line drawn by an implied hand across a printed surface the bottle physically interrupts. The rebuilt concept must not rely on backdrop line work or bands behind the centered cutout, must keep the cutout unrelit and unaltered, must add no droplets, splashes, people touching the product, or unobserved label changes, and must limit typography to one brand-name pass plus the observed category word 'REFRESCO'.
